questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement simple tenant-based access control using Kubernetes primitives and a sidecar.

## Key Concepts
- Inbound header validation
- Namespace-scoped ConfigMap as allowlist
- 403 on violations
- Structured logging for audit

## Code Example
```go
// Pseudo Go-like sketch
type Sidecar struct{ allow map[string]struct{} }
func (s *Sidecar) Handle(req *Request){
  id := req.Header.Get("X-TENANT-ID")
  if _, ok := s.allow[id]; !ok { respond403(); return }
  forward(req)
  log("tenant", id, "path", req.Path, "status", resp.Status)
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test with missing/invalid tenants?
- What are the trade-offs of moving allowlist to a central service vs ConfigMap?

Why This Is Asked

Tests practical design of a per-tenant feature flag system in a CNF gateway stack, focusing on CRD design, a lean central policy API, and a sidecar with token authentication and caching.

Key Concepts

- Kubernetes CRD for per-tenant feature flags
- Sidecar fetch with short lived token and 60s cache
- Default semantics and tenant isolation
- End-to-end test in a single namespace

Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal CRD example
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: featureflags.cnf.example.com
spec:
  group: cnf.example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              perTenantFlags:

              defaultEnabled:

    singular: featureflag
    kind: FeatureFlag
    shortNames:
    - ff
```

- How would you audit tenant flag usage and prevent leakage across tenants?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design tenant-scoped upgrades, maintain isolation, and implement progressive release with concrete mechanisms.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CRDs and multi-tenant mapping
- Canary rollouts and traffic splitting (Istio/Linkerd)
- Namespace-scoped isolation and rollback strategies
- Observability: SLIs for upgrade safety

## Code Example
```yaml
# Tenant CRD (simplified)
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: tenants.cnf.example.com
spec:
  group: cnf.example.com
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              tenantID: { type: string }
              namespace: { type: string }
              desiredVersion: { type: string }
  scope: Cluster
  names:
    plural: tenants
    singular: tenant
    kind: Tenant
    shortNames: [ tns ]
```

```yaml
# Tenant canary Deployment (tenant-a)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
        tenant: tenant-a
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: registry.example/cnf/gateway:v2
```

```yaml
# Istio TrafficSplit example for canary (tenant-a)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc.cluster.local
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc.cluster.local
        subset: v2
      weight: 10
```

kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical per-tenant traffic routing, feature flag management, and end-to-end validation with minimal manifests in CNF/Kubernetes environments.

## Key Concepts
- Sidecar-based traffic routing with per-tenant control
- Namespace-scoped ConfigMap for cnf.canary.enabled and cnf.canary.sample-rate
- Deterministic hashing for consistent bucket allocation
- Minimal YAML manifests for quick validation

## Code Example

**Namespace-scoped ConfigMap:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.canary
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  cnf.canary.enabled: "true"
  cnf.canary.sample-rate: "5"
```

**Canary Deployment:**
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: canary-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: canary
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: stable-resource
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  selector:
    app: resource
    version: stable
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

**Sidecar Configuration:**
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cnf-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: gateway
          image: cnf-gateway:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: cnf-config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: cnf-config
          configMap:
            name: cnf.canary
```

## Validation
Apply the manifests and verify routing:
```bash
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
kubectl apply -f services.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Test canary routing
export TENANT_ID="tenant-a"
for i in {1..100}; do
  curl -H "X-TENANT-ID: $TENANT_ID" http://cnf-gateway.tenant-a.svc/v2/resource
done
```

Expected: ~5% of requests route to canary-resource, 95% to stable-resource based on deterministic tenant ID hashing.
